desc: Leeds punks reinvent themselves with fiddle-driven country laments about Thatcher-era despair, an early alt-country touchstone.
Elvis Costello-produced set of raucous Irish folk-punk and Shane MacGowan's bleak ballads like 'A Pair of Brown Eyes'.
Mark E. Smith's sardonic rants over repetitive, wiry grooves, with Brix Smith adding pop hooks.
Sixties girl-group melodies buried under walls of screeching feedback and minimal drumming.
Clattering junkyard percussion, Marc Ribot's jagged guitar and Waits's growl portray New York's urban outcasts.
Polished, ambitious synth-pop exploring primal therapy themes, home to 'Shout' and 'Everybody Wants to Rule the World'.
A raw 1963 Miami club show, shelved for decades, revealing Cooke's grittier gospel-rooted side.
Spare, literate debut from the Greenwich Village folk revival, including 'Marlene on the Wall'.
Fairlight-driven art pop on side one, then 'The Ninth Wave', a suite about a woman adrift at sea.
Texan folk-country songs of small-town characters, including 'Love at the Five and Dime'.
Twangy debut blending honky-tonk with Springsteen-style rock about small-town working life.
Loud, bruising reunion with the Attractions, full of bitter break-up songs like 'I Want You'.
Organic, textured art pop with Steve Winwood's organ, bridging their synth-pop past and later post-rock.
Collection built around the Roland TR-808 electro of 'Planet Rock', which borrowed Kraftwerk melodies.
Lush, jazz-tinged quiet storm soul built around Baker's rich contralto, featuring 'Sweet Love'.
Glossy hard rock packed with sing-along hits like 'Livin' on a Prayer' and 'Wanted Dead or Alive'.
Marr's chiming guitars meet Morrissey's wry despair, including 'There Is a Light That Never Goes Out'.
Matt Johnson's politically charged, densely produced pop about Thatcher-era Britain, released alongside a full-length film.
Paul Simon's collaboration with South African musicians, fusing mbaqanga and township jive with American pop.
Todd Rundgren-produced song cycle tracing a day and a lifetime, with lush pastoral psychedelic arrangements.
Hardcore pioneers fuse punk velocity with metal, funk and soul, H.R.'s vocals soaring over it all.
Gabriel's most commercial album, with 'Sledgehammer', 'In Your Eyes' and a duet with Kate Bush.
Lyrical septet session with his band Ekaya, blending township hymns and Ellington-inspired voicings.
Kristin Hersh's fractured, tumbling songs and abrupt time shifts on 4AD's first American signing.
Steve Shelley's debut with the band, mixing alternate-tuned guitar noise with more melodic, eerie songs.
Rick Rubin-produced debut mixing heavy rock samples with bratty party rhymes; the first rap LP topping Billboard.
Stripped-down beats and scratching, including their Aerosmith collaboration 'Walk This Way'.
Dave Mustaine's technical, politically sardonic thrash, driven by David Ellefson's title-track bassline.
Twenty-nine minutes of blistering Rick Rubin-produced thrash bookended by 'Angel of Death' and 'Raining Blood'.
Bragg's songs of love and socialist politics, filled out beyond solo guitar with Johnny Marr and others.
Steve Albini's harsh guitars over a Roland drum machine, depicting small-town violence and depravity.
Complex, long-form thrash about addiction and control, the final album with bassist Cliff Burton.
Three country stars blend harmonies on traditional and contemporary songs with acoustic, bluegrass-tinged arrangements.
Arch synth-pop on Thatcher-era materialism, featuring 'It's a Sin' and a Dusty Springfield duet.
David McComb's literate, lavishly arranged songs evoking isolation and the vast Western Australian landscape.
Debut blending soul, funk and rock, with hits 'Wishing Well' and 'Sign Your Name'.
A cleaner, moodier follow-up trading feedback for reverb-soaked melancholy over a drum machine.
Michael's solo debut mixing rockabilly, funk and balladry, a huge seller with 'Faith' and 'Father Figure'.
Slovenian provocateurs recast Queen and Opus's 'Life Is Life' as martial, totalitarian-styled anthems.
The Smiths' final album, richer in arrangement, including 'Last Night I Dreamt That Somebody Loved Me'.
Rick Rubin strips the former goth band down to raw, AC/DC-style riff rock.
Philip K. Dick-inspired album with tighter songs and guitars in unconventional tunings.
East Coast thrash with hardcore punk energy and comic-book and Stephen King themes.
Quincy Jones-produced follow-up to 'Thriller', a harder-edged, synth-heavy album with five US number ones.
Andrew Eldritch's grandiose goth, with Jim Steinman's bombast, drum machine and choirs on 'This Corrosion'.
Mutt Lange's meticulously layered pop-metal, made after drummer Rick Allen lost an arm.
Darker, grander synth-pop featuring 'Never Let Me Down Again', which broke them in American stadiums.
Paul Simon-produced isicathamiya, Zulu a cappella harmonies, released after the group's Graceland exposure.
Sprawling double album spanning funk, soul, rock and gospel, written and largely played by Prince.
Eno and Lanois-produced album of chiming delay guitar and American imagery, with 'With or Without You'.
The band's final album, a double LP of melodic, noisy songs split between Bob Mould and Grant Hart.
Sharper, louder and more political, including 'The One I Love' and 'It's the End of the World'.
Raw, street-level hard rock with Slash's riffs and Axl Rose's snarl, featuring 'Sweet Child o' Mine'.
Short, extremely fast bursts of blast beats and noise, often credited with defining grindcore.
Warped psychedelic noise rock mixing sludgy riffs, tape manipulation and deranged humour, including 'Sweat Loaf'.
Live Montreux collaboration pairing Piazzolla's bandoneon quintet with Gary Burton's vibraphone.
J Mascis's drawled melodies over deafening fuzz and soaring solos, a template for 1990s alt-rock.
Owen Bradley-produced homage to 1950s Nashville countrypolitan, with guests Loretta Lynn and Brenda Lee.
Tracey Thorn and Ben Watt's understated, jazz-tinged pop of domestic memory and reflection.
Bakersfield-style honky-tonk about heartbreak and violence, produced by guitarist Pete Anderson.
Recorded live around one microphone in a Toronto church, including a slowed-down 'Sweet Jane'.
Their most polished album of jangly love songs, featuring 'Streets of Your Town'.
Mark Eitzel's despairing, literate songs of San Francisco life with spare, atmospheric arrangements.
Broadened folk-punk with Spanish and Middle Eastern touches, including 'Fairytale of New York' with Kirsty MacColl.
Martin Hannett-produced murky funk-rock with Shaun Ryder's slurred vocals, before their full dance turn.
Mike Scott's band turns to Irish traditional music, recorded largely in Dublin and Galway with fiddler Steve Wickham.
Former Slapp Happy singer interprets Hanns Eisler's political songs in German and English with sparse arrangements.
Debut album pioneering warped glide-guitar and buried, breathy vocals that defined shoegaze.
Morrissey's solo debut after the Smiths, with Vini Reilly's guitar and 'Everyday Is Like Sunday'.
Perry Farrell's yelp over Dave Navarro's metal riffs and funky, psychedelic grooves, including 'Jane Says'.
Sub Pop release of sludgy, fuzz-pedal garage punk that helped define the early Seattle grunge sound.
LA band fusing ska, funk, punk and metal, including a cover of Curtis Mayfield's 'Freddie's Dead'.
Vernon Reid's virtuosic guitar leads funk-metal songs on race and politics, including 'Cult of Personality'.
Icelandic debut fronted by Björk's elastic voice, featuring the indie hit 'Birthday'.
Catchy melodies drowned in fuzz, including 'Freak Scene', recorded as the original lineup splintered.
First major-label album, mixing bright pop like 'Stand' and 'Orange Crush' with mandolin-led reflections.
Cohen's deep voice over cheap synthesizers on sardonic songs like 'First We Take Manhattan'.
Spare acoustic songs about poverty and resilience, including 'Fast Car' and 'Talkin' 'bout a Revolution'.
Double album of long, alternate-tuned guitar epics like 'Teen Age Riot', drifting between melody and noise.
The Bomb Squad's dense, noisy sample collages carry Chuck D's political rhymes and Flavor Flav's interjections.
Dr. Dre and DJ Yella's funk-sampled beats behind confrontational street narratives and a protest against police brutality.
Steve Albini-recorded debut album of loud-quiet dynamics, Black Francis's screams and 'Where Is My Mind?'.
Long, intricate thrash with a notoriously thin bass mix, including the anti-war 'One'.
Madonna's most personal record, mixing gospel choirs, funk and confessional songs about family and faith.
Kravitz plays most instruments on a retro blend of 1960s rock, soul and psychedelia.
Swaggering mix of rap, pop and club beats, including 'Buffalo Stance' and 'Manchild'.
Glossy hard-rock comeback with horns and hooks, including 'Love in an Elevator' and 'Janie's Got a Gun'.
Partly recorded in Ibiza, blending Balearic acid house beats with guitar-led melancholy pop.
Don Was-produced comeback of mature, slide-guitar-flecked pop-blues that swept the Grammys.
Jazzie B's sound-system crew pair laid-back hip hop beats with strings and soul vocals, including 'Back to Life'.
Ferocious, compressed thrash-jazz readings of Ornette Coleman tunes for two altos and two drummers.
Native Tongues pioneers mixing Afrocentric themes and jazz samples, plus the house crossover 'I'll House You'.
Mike Patton's debut with the band fuses metal, funk, rap and keyboards, including 'Epic'.
Shimmering guitar psychedelia over loose, funky drums, ending with the extended groove of 'I Am the Resurrection'.
Intimate acoustic duets drawing on Senegal's Fula traditions, carried by Maal's soaring voice.
Lush art pop with uilleann pipes and Bulgarian choir, opening with a song inspired by Molly Bloom.
Cut-and-paste sampling duo's debut with guests Lisa Stansfield and Yazz, rooted in early UK club culture.
Comeback featuring guests Carlos Santana, Bonnie Raitt and others around Hooker's hypnotic boogie.
Jam and Lewis-produced, industrial-tinged new jack swing with socially conscious themes and a string of hit singles.
Prince Paul-produced debut of whimsical skits and eclectic samples from Steely Dan to Hall & Oates.
Manchester acid house featuring 'Pacific State', with its saxophone line and birdsong samples.
Debut blending hip hop, house and reggae, including the feminist anthem 'Ladies First' with Monie Love.
Long, slow, synth-swathed songs of despair and love, including 'Pictures of You' and 'Lovesong'.
Gil Norton-produced album of surreal, catchy songs with loud-quiet dynamics, including 'Debaser' and 'Monkey Gone to Heaven'.
Mike Watt and George Hurley's post-Minutemen band in a loose, jazzy, bass-forward punk mode.
Swiss trio replacing guitars with samplers, mixing industrial noise with cabaret and classical fragments.
Minimalist, drone-based psychedelia with organ hymns and the repetitive 'Revolution'.
Former Magazine bassist's score for an imaginary black-and-white noir film, mixing jazz, strings and samples.
Dust Brothers-produced collage of hundreds of samples, a dense, funky rethink after their brash debut.
Lee Mavers's retro Merseybeat songs, including 'There She Goes', on an album he publicly disowned.
Harold Faltermeyer-produced analogue-synth album of quiet, reflective songs on ageing, love and loss.
Taut post-hardcore with dub-influenced bass and anti-consumerist themes from Dischord's flagship band.
Paul Oakenfold and Steve Osborne-produced baggy dance-rock, including 'Step On' and 'Kinky Afro'.
Their most accessible album, Liz Fraser's clearer, soaring vocals over shimmering, layered guitars.
Introspective, stripped-back album, including 'Freedom! '90' and 'Praying for Time'.
Kitschy, funk-sampled club pop featuring 'Groove Is in the Heart' with Bootsy Collins.
Debut album of surging, effects-laden guitars, propulsive drums and hazy harmonies, including 'Vapour Trail'.
Major-label debut with tighter, catchier noise rock, including 'Kool Thing' with Chuck D.
P-Funk-sampling concept album about a fictional drug, featuring 'The Humpty Dance'.
Hard-rocking first half, then long orchestrated epics like 'Three Days'; includes 'Been Caught Stealing'.
Personal, emotionally raw album featuring her version of Prince's 'Nothing Compares 2 U'.
Marley Marl-produced comeback, from the title track's aggression to the smooth 'Around the Way Girl'.
Long, loose and noisy guitar jams recorded live with Crazy Horse, anticipating grunge.
Flood-produced, sleek and minimal synth-pop featuring 'Personal Jesus' and 'Enjoy the Silence'.
Solo debut produced with Public Enemy's Bomb Squad, mixing West Coast narratives with East Coast noise.
Surf guitar and outer-space themes on a smoother, more atmospheric album than its predecessors.
Dense Bomb Squad sample collages tackling race and media, including 'Fight the Power' and '911 Is a Joke'.
Retro Southern rock debut channelling the Faces and Stones, including a cover of 'Hard to Handle'.
Scottish indie band turned rave act, merging acid house, rap and psychedelia, including 'Move Any Mountain'.
Playful, jazz- and rock-sampled debut, including 'Can I Kick It?' and 'Bonita Applebum'.
Technically intricate thrash with Marty Friedman's lead guitar, including 'Holy Wars' and 'Hangar 18'.
Big Star-style harmonies over fuzzed guitars, including 'The Concept'.
Bristol sound-system collective's debut blending hip hop, dub and soul, featuring 'Unfinished Sympathy'.
Finn brothers' harmonies on melodic songs including 'Weather With You' and 'Four Seasons in One Day'.
Stadium house anthems like '3 a.m. Eternal' and 'Last Train to Trancentral' linked by ambient interludes.
Partly recorded in Berlin, a reinvention using industrial textures and dance rhythms, featuring 'One'.
Lo-fi garage grunge recorded on eight-track, including 'Let It Slide'.
Former PiL bassist mixes dub bass with North African and Celtic influences, with Sinéad O'Connor guest vocals.
